beats.act: OPEN
beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask answered, Vedanshu signs in
beats.narration_text: Shalom — I'm Vedanshu Daxesh Patel. Chapter two left one requirement unmet: hand the model the right text. This film is about the word hiding inside that sentence — "right." A computer can't tell if two pieces of text mean the same thing just by reading them. Six acts: word vectors, a famous trick that almost works, whole passages, an old idea called cosine similarity, a worked example that decides everything, and why none of it needs matching words.

props.command: Explain how a computer decides whether two pieces of text mean the same thing — from raw word vectors, through a famous trick that almost works, to the worked example that proves meaning beats vocabulary.
output: vector arithmetic — with a real caveat
worked example: same words, different meaning

beats.act: I — From Words To Numbers
beats.role_note: ACT I open — substantive claim beat (no bare card, matches sibling precedent)
beats.narration_text: Act one: a computer doesn't understand words, sentences, or meaning — only numbers. So the first move in modern language processing is turning text into a vector: a list of numbers, not arbitrary, but learned, so the numbers carry something real about what the text means.

show.event: Headline types in: "Turn text into numbers — learned, not assigned."
Subline resolves: A computer can't read for meaning. The first move is a vector: numbers that carry something real about the text.
Spark line settles: Learned, not arbitrary.

beats.act: I — From Words To Numbers
beats.narration_text: Zoom into a single page. Word2vec trains a neural network over a corpus of 1.6 billion words — Mikolov and colleagues, 2013 — learning, for every word, a few hundred numbers.

beats.act: I — From Words To Numbers
beats.narration_text: Nobody hand-assigns these numbers — the network discovers them from which words appear near which others. Plotted in two dimensions: "vacation," "PTO," "leave" cluster together; "printer" sits far off. A teaching simplification — real embeddings use hundreds of dimensions.

production_viz.note: Mikolov et al. 2013; two dimensions only for teaching, real vectors have hundreds

beats.act: I — From Words To Numbers

beats.act: II — The Trick That Almost Works
beats.narration_text: Take the vector for "king." Subtract "man." Add "woman." The result lands close to the vector for "queen" — Mikolov, Yih, and Zweig, 2013. Not the raw positions — the *directions* between vectors encode relationships.

Subline resolves: Not the raw positions — the directions between vectors encode relationships (Mikolov, Yih & Zweig, 2013).
Spark line settles: Directions carry meaning too.

beats.act: II — The Trick That Almost Works
beats.narration_text: Here's the honest part: run the naive search for the nearest vector, and it often lands back on "king" itself. Later replication work found the trick only works once you exclude the query word from the search.

beats.act: III — From Words To Whole Passages
beats.narration_text: Word2vec operates one word at a time — clean, but not what a RAG system actually embeds. A help-desk question is a whole passage, and a passage's meaning is more than the sum of its words.

a full sentence of word-points appears beside it, loosely scattered
the sentence's points pull toward one new combined point: 'a passage, one vector'

production_viz.label: the word-level to passage-level gap the chapter opens Act III on
production_viz.mechanic: individual word-points contrasted with, then merged into, one whole-passage point
production_viz.note: framing beat only — no invented numbers, sets up BERT/Sentence-BERT

beats.act: III — From Words To Whole Passages
beats.narration_text: Getting from word-level vectors to whole-passage vectors took a further step. Transformer models like BERT learn deep, contextual representations of text — Devlin and colleagues, 2019.

beats.act: III — From Words To Whole Passages
beats.narration_text: But BERT's raw output, used directly, compares whole sentences poorly. Sentence-BERT restructures the same network so a passage becomes one vector, meaningful to compare directly against others — Reimers and Gurevych, 2019.

card restructures — 'Sentence-BERT' label draws over the same network shape
two sentence-vectors compared again, marked reliable, direct comparison arrow

production_viz.label: BERT's raw output vs. Sentence-BERT's restructured output for sentence comparison
production_viz.mechanic: one state-card morphing into a second, same architecture rewired for a different comparison

beats.act: III — From Words To Whole Passages
beats.narration_text: The efficiency case is not subtle: finding the most similar pair among ten thousand sentences takes roughly sixty-five hours with raw BERT. With Sentence-BERT: about five seconds, at comparable accuracy.

bar 2 lands tiny: 'Sentence-BERT — ~5 seconds'

beats.act: IV — Closeness As Meaning, An Old Idea
beats.narration_text: Long before neural embeddings, information retrieval already represented documents and queries as vectors — a card catalog for meaning, built out of raw term counts.

show.event: wide shot: a wall of old library card-catalog drawers

shot.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md.

beats.act: IV — Closeness As Meaning, An Old Idea
beats.narration_text: Pull one drawer. Cosine similarity — the cosine of the angle between two vectors — was already the standard way to score how alike two of these vectors were, independent of length. Manning, Raghavan, and Schütze, 2008.

show.event: tight shot: one open drawer, index cards fanned, hand pulling one card

shot.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent) — same plate family as B17. See SHOPPING.md.

beats.act: IV — Closeness As Meaning, An Old Idea
beats.narration_text: The geometry itself: two vectors, an angle between them. Small angle, cosine near one, close in meaning. Wide angle, cosine near zero, unrelated. Embeddings didn't invent this measure — they gave it a far richer vector to work on.

show.event: two vectors draw from the origin; angle θ arcs between them
θ shrinks; label 'cos θ → 1, close in meaning'
θ widens toward 90°; label 'cos θ → 0, unrelated'

production_viz.label: cosine similarity as the angle between two vectors
production_viz.mechanic: an animated angle sweep between two vectors with cos θ labeled at each extreme
production_viz.note: Manning, Raghavan & Schütze 2008; the formula, not a computed example

beats.act: IV — Closeness As Meaning, An Old Idea
beats.narration_text: That's the honest lineage: cosine similarity predates embeddings by decades. What changed is not how closeness gets measured — it's what kind of vector gets fed into the measurement.

show.event: Headline types in: "An old tool, a new vector."
Subline resolves: Cosine similarity predates embeddings by decades. What changed is the vector fed into it, not the measurement itself.
Spark line settles: The ruler didn't change. What it measures did.

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap the whole film. Text becomes a vector, learned from patterns in ordinary language, not assigned by hand — word2vec proved it at scale (Mikolov et al., 2013). Vector arithmetic hints at real structure, but only once you exclude the query word from the search. Whole passages need Sentence-BERT, not raw BERT, to compare well (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019). Cosine similarity, the tool that measures closeness, predates embeddings by decades (Manning, Raghavan, and Schütze, 2008). And the whole point: two questions can share almost no words and mean the same thing, or share a whole phrase and mean nothing alike. The vector captures meaning. Not vocabulary.

beats.act: your turn
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'Give me three short phrases about the same general topic, written so two of them mean nearly the same thing in very different words, and one of them shares a lot of literal wording with one of the first two but means something different. Tell me, using reasoning about meaning and not any computation, which two you'd expect to land closest together in embedding space, and why.' Try it on a topic you actually know well, and see if Claude's reasoning matches your own intuition about what 'means the same thing' actually requires.
